summary.text: The instrumental temperature record is the record of Earth's air and ocean temperatures built from direct measurements.
Reliable series began in some regions between 1850 and 1880, with data coming mainly from weather stations and satellites.
Its rising global surface temperature is one of many lines of evidence that human activities are causing climate change.

items.prompt: Global temperature rose before 1940, then held fairly steady until about 1970 before climbing again. What has the mid-century pause mostly been blamed on?

options.label: A run of unusually cold winters
Sulfate aerosols in the air
Fewer weather stations reporting
A dip in the Sun's brightness

items.explain: The cooling or plateau from 1940 to 1970 has been mostly attributed to sulfate aerosol.

items.prompt: From 1850–1900 to 2011–2020, which warmed more: the continents or the oceans?

options.label: The sea surface, by about double
Both warmed by the same amount
Air over land, by nearly double
Neither changed noticeably

items.explain: Land air temperatures rose about 1.59 °C while sea surface temperatures rose about 0.88 °C.

items.prompt: A skeptic argues that warming in the global record is just cities heating up around thermometers. What do the measurements suggest?

options.label: City heat explains most of the warming
City heat is corrected by ignoring land data
Cities have cooled the record overall
Uncorrected city effects likely add under 10%

items.explain: It is unlikely that uncorrected urbanisation or land-use effects raised global land warming by more than 10%, though some fast-growing regions show local signals.

items.prompt: One year runs warmer than the trend and the next runs cooler, even as the long-term line keeps rising. What can cause such ups and downs?

options.label: Natural swings such as El Niño
Thermometers being swapped each year
Satellites measuring only the poles
The record skipping alternate years

items.explain: Within the upward trend, some variability comes from natural internal swings such as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation.

items.prompt: To build the global surface temperature, scientists combine sea surface and land air readings. How are the two parts weighted?

options.label: Equally, half and half
By how many people live there
By the area each covers
By how many stations each has

items.explain: Global surface temperature combines sea surface and land air temperatures, weighted by their respective areas.

items.prompt: Scientists want temperatures from 500 years ago, long before thermometers were common. What can they use?

options.label: Weather balloon launches
Tree rings and ice cores
Old satellite photographs
Ocean heat content data

items.explain: For the distant past, proxy data from tree rings, corals and ice cores can stand in for direct measurements.
